newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's AIDS vaccine goal daunting, but reachable.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's AIDS vaccine goal daunting, but reachable.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's goal of finding an AIDS vaccine in the next 10 years is a daunting challenge, but some advocates say that with enough money and a possible breakthrough, it might be done.
"The goal of developing a vaccine is achievable," Dr. Arthur Ammann, president of the American Foundation for Aids Research (AMFAR) said in an interview. "The time is hard to pin down."
Clinton promised on Sunday that the United States would find an AIDS vaccine within a decade, likening the challenge to the Kennedy era's quest to put an American on the moon in the 1960s.

He said a special research centre will be set up at the National Institutes of Health, adding $17 million to U.S. AIDS spending and bringing the annual total to $150 million, which some activists consider inadequate to address all facets of the AIDS epidemic.

"We applaud the president's commitment but stress that this project will require a large infusion of federal money, which must not be siphoned from other programmes that support people with HIV and AIDS," said Winnie Stachelberg, legislative director of Human Rights Campaign, a gay rights lobby.
These other programmes include continued research into drug treatments and a cure, as well as social service programmes for people with AIDS, the group said in a statement.

Dr. June Osborn, who chaired the U.S. Commission on AIDS from 1989-1993, was sceptical that a vaccine could be created at all, let alone by 2007, given previous frustrating efforts to pin down the wily virus.

"I think more resources are absolutely indicated," Osborn said by telephone from New York. She noted that AIDS researchers have been toiling since the mid-1980s and have been thwarted in their search for a vaccine. "I think one has to be in awe of the problem."

Central to the task is the very nature of the disease, Osborn said. The virus mutates so quickly that a vaccine that seems effective one day might not be the next. In addition, she said, the human immune system's inability to make any anti-bodies to fight HIV made the search for vaccines even more difficult.

Gregg Gonsalves of the New York-based Treatment Action Group, which has pushed hard for expedited federal approval of AIDS drugs, was encouraged by the Clinton plan but echoed Osborn's concern about scientific obstacles.
Budget-cutting zeal in Washington could be another hurdle, Gonsalves said, if it targets the National Institutes of Health, which includes the prime government research facility for AIDS.

Without a vaccine, experts say AIDS will soon overtake tuberculosis and malaria as the leading killer disease of people aged 25-to-44. Some 3 million people are infected with HIV each year and 29 million carry the virus.
AMFAR's Ammann acknowledged problems, but said the short history of AIDS in the United States had proved past Cassandras wrong.

"At the beginning we were very pessimistic about finding the cause of AIDS; then we found the virus in 1985," Ammann said from his office in San Rafael, Calif. "A lot of people said we'd never find a treatment, and now we have 11 treatments."

He said another "impossible goal" was the prevention of transmission of HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, from pregnant women to their babies, and noted this goal was achieved in 1994 with the use of the drug AZT.

Both Osborn and Ammann cited a perception that resources for AIDS prevention had been outpaced by funds to find treatments and a cure. Osborn also said researchers had known for years how to prevent the spread of AIDS: educate the public about risky behaviours such as unprotected sex or the sharing of needles by intravenous drug users.
The end-goal must be kept in view, Osborn said.
"We're not doing this to make a vaccine, we're doing this to prevent AIDS, and that's the important thing."
